title: Ribbon OEM Supplier Shortlist Scoring and Cost Validity
meta_desc: How to score a ribbon OEM supplier shortlist and test whether quoted costs are valid, comparable and complete before you commit a private label programme.
og_desc: A practical method for scoring a ribbon OEM shortlist and validating quoted costs: comparable quotes, hidden cost lines, weighting and weighted scorecards.
tw_desc: How to score a ribbon OEM supplier shortlist and check that quoted costs are valid and comparable before committing a private label ribbon programme.
kpi: Most shortlists fail in the same way. Everyone on the list is scored on the criteria that are easy to measure, and the criteria that decide whether the programme works are left until after an award has been made. Scoring should not reward a supplier for sending a complete quotation. It should tell you which supplier you can place a repeat order with, and whether the number in the quotation is a number you can plan against.

faq: How many suppliers should a ribbon OEM shortlist contain?

Three to five. Below three you have no comparison and you will end up negotiating against yourself. Above five the reviews consume more time than the programme justifies, and the suppliers at the bottom of the list rarely become serious candidates - they are there as padding. The practical pattern is four suppliers: two strong candidates, one who may be commercially attractive but operationally unproven, and one who is your benchmark on price and service even if you will not place the order with them.
What makes a ribbon quotation valid for comparison?

Three things: the specification is written to the same level of detail in every quotation, the price basis and Incoterm are stated explicitly, and the quantities are identical. If one supplier quotes a 10mm printed polyester satin ribbon and another quotes a 12mm woven grosgrain, their numbers are not comparable at any level of analysis - no percentage normalisation makes them so. When you issue the request for quotation, specify every field you need priced, mark each as mandatory, and ask each supplier to state that they have priced against that specification. If a supplier cannot price a mandatory field, that is a shortlist data point, not a clarification request.
Should cost be weighted most heavily in the scoring, or should quality and capability dominate?

It depends on whether the programme is a first order or an extension. For a first order in an unfamiliar category, capability and quality should carry the most weight, because a low price from a supplier who cannot hold your standard is not a saving - it is a defect cost with a delay attached. For an established programme with a proven supplier, cost can carry more weight because the operational risk is already known and priced into the relationship. The mistake is using the same weighting for every situation, which systematically under-weights the risk you are actually carrying.
What cost lines are most commonly missing from a ribbon quotation?

Decoration tooling and setup charges are the most frequent omission, because some factories treat them as one-off and some treat them as recurring. Others include: colour development and lab dip fees, sample and prototype costs, packaging development, testing and certification, freight and insurance beyond the stated Incoterm, and the cost of sorting or rework that the factory assumes it will absorb. Ask for a line-by-line price build-up and a written statement of which charges are one-time and which recur. Then convert everything to a single figure per unit at your actual annual volume, including amortising setup across the number of orders you realistically place per year.
How much weight should I give the lowest price, even when it is significantly cheaper?

Treat an outlier low price as a question, not as a win. The most useful question is what is different about that supplier's specification, service level or cost structure - and the second most useful is asking them to confirm the price against a stated volume with a validity period. Price differences of a few percent between comparable quotes are usually real efficiency. Differences of twenty to thirty percent almost always mean a different specification, a different service scope or a different risk appetite, and the quote should not be accepted until you know which. Awarding on headline price without that diagnosis is how a programme ends up with a supplier who cannot hold the standard you signed for.
How should the scorecard outcome be used, and what happens to the runner-up?

Use the weighted score to structure the decision and to identify the weak dimension of the leading supplier, then verify that dimension before awarding. If the winner scores highest but has a clearly weaker capacity or compliance position, that gap needs a specific mitigation - a documented schedule, a second source, a contractual remedy - and if it cannot be mitigated, the second supplier may be the better award. The runner-up is worth maintaining deliberately: a scored shortlist gives you the evidence to keep a credible alternative warm, which is what makes a mid-programme change of supplier survivable rather than a crisis.
